passage:
For a long time people assumed that bees belonged in the countryside, among fields and orchards. Recent studies have overturned that idea. In several European cities, hives placed on rooftops have produced more honey per year than hives in nearby farmland.

The reason lies in what grows around them. Modern farms often plant a single crop across huge areas. When that crop finishes flowering, the bees have nothing left to feed on for weeks. A city, by contrast, is a patchwork of small gardens, parks, balconies and roadside trees, and these are planted with many different species. Something is almost always in bloom, so the supply of food is steady rather than sudden.

Temperature helps too. Buildings, roads and pavements absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, keeping cities warmer than the land around them. Bees emerge earlier in spring and remain active later into the autumn, which lengthens the season in which they can collect nectar.

Pesticides are the third factor. Farmers spray chemicals to protect their crops, and these treatments can weaken or kill bees. Gardeners in cities use far less spray, and many use none at all.

City beekeeping is not without difficulties. Space is limited, and a hive on a rooftop can be hard to reach and hard to inspect. Some cities have seen so many new hives appear that beekeepers worry the available flowers cannot support them all. Even so, the number of urban hives continues to rise, and the honey they produce is often sold within a few streets of where it was made.
